beginner.headline: Students Protest for Better Schools in France
beginner.brief: Crowds of mainly teenagers called for more resources for schools. They also wanted an end to what they called police repression. A wave of protests by high-school pupils spread to their parents, university students and unions. Police clashed with demonstrators in Lyon. Police used tear gas in Paris and Marseille. The government said that 215 students and 85 staff had been hurt. Alissa, a student, said that schools were falling apart. Her friend, Sacha, said the ceilings in Marseille's schools were leaking and conditions were poor. Students will keep protesting until good measures are taken.

intermediate.headline: School Demonstrations Grow Across France Over Conditions and Police Actions
intermediate.brief: Tear gas was used in Paris and Marseille as school demonstrations increased across France. Large gatherings of mostly teenagers demanded better funding for schools and an end to what they called severe actions by officers. Hundreds of thousands of people joined the street actions across France, with high-school pupils, parents, university students, and unions participating. Police encountered demonstrators in Lyon and used tear gas in Paris and Marseille. The government stated that 891 high schools experienced disruption on Tuesday, representing almost a quarter of all lycées. Students explained that school buildings were often dilapidated, with leaking ceilings making it difficult to study. Official offers, such as a website for students to express their grievances, have made little impact so far. There is significant worry about claims of "disproportionate force" used by officers, with investigations now ongoing. A 14-year-old student suffered a fractured jaw and lost teeth after being hit in the face during a school blockade. What began with local anger at overcrowded classrooms and dilapidated school buildings has since extended across the country, reaching some universities.

advanced.headline: French School Demonstrations Intensify: Demands for Reform and Police Concerns
advanced.brief: Tear gas was used in Paris and Marseille as school protests grew across France. Initially, crowds consisting mainly of teenagers called for more resources for schools and an end to what they characterized as police repression. Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France, as a wave of protests by high-school pupils spread to their parents, university students and unions. The government reported that over 250,000 demonstrators participated on Tuesday, with disruptions in almost a quarter of all lycées. Students' unions, however, claimed significantly higher numbers, putting total demonstrators at 450,000 and blockaded high schools at 1,800 on what the protesters dubbed "Act Three" of their movement. Police clashed with demonstrators in Lyon, using tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes, though serious trouble was less severe than in previous protests. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned earlier violence, reporting 215 students, 85 staff, and 715 police officers had been hurt since the protests began. Education Minister Édouard Geffray appealed for dialogue over school blockades and warned against "ultra-violent elements" infiltrating student movements. Student accounts, such as Alissa's from Marseille, describe schools as "falling apart," necessitating their presence in street protests. Her friend, Sacha, further detailed poor conditions, including leaking ceilings in Marseille's schools, hindering effective study. Widespread concern exists over allegations of "disproportionate force" by police, with France's IGPN police inspectorate investigating multiple cases. One police officer has been charged by prosecutors with "violence... resulting in mutilation or permanent disability" after firing a tear-gas grenade at a high school student. Another alarming incident involved a 15-year-old's hand being torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near a school in Lens. Government efforts, including a website for grievances and internal school discussions, have made little impression on the students so far. With further union-backed mobilisations anticipated, the current wave of discontent appears unlikely to abate in the near future. One couple in their 70s, Alain and Michèle, joined the march in central Paris, to show their support for young students, explaining that as former teachers they understood the problems that France's education system was facing.
